blocks.content: Glaciers move under the force of gravity through internal plastic deformation and basal sliding.

rows: Glacier body slides over bedrock on a water film
Ice crystals slip and re-align under immense pressure
Occurs in both cold-based and warm-based glaciers
Controlled by basal water pressure and bed roughness
Controlled by ice temperature and cumulative ice mass pressure

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Glaciers move downward under the influence of gravity through internal deformation and basal sliding.
Internal plastic deformation occurs deep within the glacier where high pressure forces ice crystals to slide past one another.
Basal sliding is facilitated by thin layers of meltwater acting as a lubricant between the bedrock and the glacial base.
The rigid upper layer (top 50 meters) lacks sufficient pressure for plastic deformation, leading to fracture and crevasse formation.
Glacial velocity is highest at the center and surface due to reduced friction compared to the sides and bottom.
Crevasses only form in the brittle zone above 50 meters depth; below this depth, plastic flow seals cracks.
Warm-based (temperate) glaciers move significantly faster than cold-based (polar) glaciers due to basal meltwater lubricant.
Glacial surges refer to short-lived events where movement speed increases up to 100 times normal rates.
